steps.action:
# The Light Between

The fog came in like a held breath.

Maren had learned to read it over thirty-one years at Gull Point — the way it moved differently depending on the season, the way it tasted different on a November night versus a June morning. November fog was heavy and purposeful, the kind that settled into your collar and stayed. June fog was apologetic, thin and lacy, gone by eight o'clock. This fog, arriving on the last Wednesday of October, was neither. It had a weight to it that she couldn't categorize, and after thirty-one years, an uncategorized fog was the most interesting thing that could happen to a person.

She climbed the stairs the way she always climbed them — one hand trailing the curved iron railing, counting without meaning to. Eighty-two steps. She had counted them on her first night at the lighthouse and every night since, the way you might say a prayer not because you doubt God but because the words themselves are a comfort. Eighty-two steps, and at the top, the light.

The Fresnel lens had been there since 1887. It was a thing of extraordinary beauty — concentric rings of glass prisms arranged in a beehive shape, designed to gather the lamp's light and throw it outward in a focused beam instead of letting it scatter uselessly into the dark. The principle was French and over a century old and it worked better than almost anything else humans had ever invented for the purpose. Maren polished it every third day with a cloth so soft it felt like touching nothing. She had worn out eleven such cloths. She kept the worn ones in a box under her cot, though she couldn't have explained why.

She checked the lamp, made her notes in the logbook, and stood at the glass for a while, looking out at the nothing.

*November 1, 0200 hours. Fog, dense. Visibility approximately 50 yards. All systems operating. Wind from the northeast at 8 knots. No vessel traffic observed.*

No vessel traffic observed. She wrote that phrase most nights. Occasionally she wondered if it was the saddest sentence in the English language, and then she decided it wasn't, because sadness requires expectation, and she had given up expecting vessels a long time ago.

---

She had taken the posting at twenty-six, right after her mother died, because she needed somewhere to be alone that wasn't the apartment where her mother had been sick. The lighthouse seemed like a practical solution to an emotional problem, which was the only kind of solution Maren trusted. The woman from the maritime authority had warned her: it's remote, there's no society to speak of, the winters are brutal, the work is largely mechanical, and there's precious little to recommend it to someone of your age.

"I'll take it," Maren said.

She had expected to stay two years. Then three. Then she stopped counting years the way the lighthouse made her count stairs — involuntarily, automatically, as a kind of background process that didn't require her conscious attention.

She had lovers over the years, all of them people who had initially found her solitude romantic and eventually found it maddening. One of them, a marine biologist named Patrick who smelled perpetually of salt water even when he hadn't been near the ocean, had lasted almost four years. He used to take the supply boat out to visit her for stretches of two and three weeks, and she had loved those weeks — the particular pleasure of having a person in a space that was usually only large enough for herself. But when he asked her to leave the lighthouse, to come back to the mainland and live like a regular person, she discovered that she couldn't do it the same way she discovered she couldn't eat shellfish: not with regret but with a kind of bodily certainty that this simply was not for her.

"You love that tower more than you love me," he said.

"I don't think that's it," she said, which was not exactly a denial.

After Patrick there was no one else who lasted. She didn't mourn this. You can only mourn what you actually wanted, and what Maren wanted was to be the person between the light and the dark, to be useful in a way that required no approval, to send her beam out into the fog every night regardless of whether any ship was there to receive it. She found this satisfying in a way she had never found anything else satisfying, and she had learned enough about herself to know that this was not ordinary, and that ordinary was not something she had ever successfully been.

---

On this particular October night, at approximately two-forty in the morning, she heard a sound.

It was not a sound she could immediately identify, which was alarming, because she had catalogued every sound at Gull Point with the same thoroughness she had catalogued the fog. There was the groan of the iron railing when the temperature dropped below forty. There was the particular cry of the murres nesting on the north face of the rocks, which could sound disturbingly human in the right wind. There was the supply boat's engine, a flatulent diesel rumble she could distinguish from half a mile. There was the foghorn, which was her own voice in a sense, a voice she had inherited from the keeper before her.

This sound was not any of those sounds.

She went out onto the gallery — the narrow iron walkway that ringed the lamp room — and the fog received her like a cold room. She held the railing and looked down at the rocks. The beam swept around every four seconds, and in the illuminated instants she could see the water below, black and fractured, and between the rocks something pale.

She looked for a long time.

She went down eighty-two stairs. She pulled on her oilskin coat and took the lantern from its hook by the door, the battery-powered one she used for night walks on the rocks. She went down the path to the water's edge.

It was a dog.

A large white dog, the breed she couldn't name, draped across a flat rock just above the waterline. It was not dead — she could see the sides moving — but it was utterly exhausted, the way an animal looks when it has given everything and arrived on the other side of everything and found itself inexplicably still alive. It looked up at her with eyes the color of amber and made no sound.

Maren knelt on the wet rock. She put her hand on the dog's side and felt the heart going — fast, terrified, determined.

"All right," she said. "All right, now."

She was not a person who talked to animals as a rule. She was not much of a person who talked at all. But something about the fog and the hour and the amber eyes made it seem necessary to establish certain facts out loud.

"I'm going to need to carry you," she said. "You're going to have to let me."

She didn't know how the dog had gotten there. The nearest vessel she'd logged in three days was a container ship that had passed six miles out. It didn't matter how. What mattered was the same thing that always mattered: something had come through the dark and arrived, and she was here.

She was stronger than she looked. Thirty-one years of carrying fuel canisters and supply boxes up eighty-two stairs tends to develop a specific kind of practical strength in a person, the kind that isn't impressive in a gymnasium but is very useful at two-forty in the morning on a wet rock. She got the dog up in both arms — it must have weighed eighty pounds — and carried it up the path.

Inside, she set it on the braided rug in front of the woodstove and lit the stove. She got water in a low bowl and held it close. The dog drank without lifting its head, which she recognized as the behavior of a creature that cannot tell the difference yet between desperate thirst and the possibility of safety, that cannot spare the energy to make the distinction. She understood this. She had felt it herself, once.

She sat on the floor with her back against the cot and her hand on the dog's ribs and she stayed there until the ribs stopped heaving and the breathing slowed and the amber eyes closed.

Outside, the light kept turning.

---

By morning the dog could stand, which Maren took to be a good sign. By afternoon it had eaten — she had tinned fish, which it accepted with the grave dignity of an animal that has decided not to die. By the following morning it followed her up the eighty-two stairs and stood at the gallery railing beside her and looked out at the water with a seriousness that she found appropriate.

She called the maritime authority and reported finding the animal. She called the one veterinarian who served the coastal district, a practical woman named Dr. Suárez who came out on the supply boat three days later and examined the dog and found him healthy, if recently traumatized, and male, and between three and five years old, and microchipped, the chip belonging to a sailing vessel called *Meridian* that had gone down in a storm off the cape eleven days earlier. The two crew members had been rescued. The dog, apparently, had been listed in the report as lost.

"You'll want me to contact the owners," Dr. Suárez said.

Maren looked at the dog, who was sitting at her feet looking at the lens with apparent interest.

"Yes," she said.

Dr. Suárez made some calls. The owners had survived the wreck of the *Meridian* and were safe in a harbor town sixty miles up the coast. They were grateful beyond expression that the dog was alive. They wanted to come for him immediately.

"Of course," Maren said.

She had four days with the dog before the owners arrived on the supply boat. She did not name him, on the grounds that it wasn't her place to name a thing that already belonged somewhere. She took him up the stairs every night and stood with him on the gallery while the beam turned. He seemed to understand the purpose of the light — or perhaps he understood her purpose, which came to the same thing. Either way, he stood with his nose lifted into the wind and she stood beside him and they watched the dark water together.

When the owners came — a young couple, windburned and watery-eyed, the woman not yet able to say the dog's name without crying — Maren stood at the dock and watched them kneel on the weathered boards and the dog went to them without hesitation, without a backward look, which was the correct and proper thing to do.

She stood there until the supply boat was out of sight.

Then she went back up to the lighthouse, because the light had no opinions about any of this and still needed keeping. She climbed the stairs, counting without meaning to. Eighty-two. She checked the lamp. She made her notes.

*Clear. Visibility unlimited. Wind from the southwest at 12 knots. No vessel traffic observed.*

She stood at the lens for a while with her hand resting on the glass the way she might rest a hand on a shoulder — her own gesture of continuance, of still being there. Below her, the rocks were wet and empty and the ocean moved in its slow, enormous way, indifferent as ever.

She thought: the light doesn't know if anyone is out there. The light just goes.

This had always been enough for her. It was still enough.

She went down the stairs to make her supper, counting backward this time, for no reason at all.
